extracted.intended_audience: graduate students, early-career researchers, and mathematicians doing research
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for doing original mathematical research emphasizing attitude and long-term practices (patience, strategic work selection, steady learning) rather than specific technical methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extended time investment
rubrics_metrics.description: "Any given problem generally requires months of effort" to achieve meaningful progress; breakthroughs require patient elimination of unsuccessful approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to spend months (or longer) on a single problem; progress is typically the result of iteratively discarding ideas that don't work rather than one sudden trick. Plan for long-term engagement and repeated attempts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of slow progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Long periods without visible advancement are normal and enable later faster completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect and tolerate stretches with little apparent progress; such incubation periods are part of productive research and often precede bursts of completion. Do not judge research worth solely by short-term visible gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic deferral
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting aside difficult problems temporarily — while continuing related work — allows skill development before returning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When stuck, consciously defer the problem and use the time to work on related, more tractable problems that build relevant skills or intuition; return later with improved tools rather than stubbornly forcing immediate resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rarity of eureka moments
rubrics_metrics.description: Most advances result from consistent, thoughtful effort, not sudden inspiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on expecting 'eureka' insights; instead cultivate steady, disciplined work habits that accumulate understanding and lead to incremental advances that combine into major progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility about breakthroughs
rubrics_metrics.description: Be skeptical of solutions that seem "too easy"; they may overlook real difficulties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat apparently simple solutions with caution: thoroughly check for overlooked cases, hidden assumptions, or gaps. Use peer feedback and detailed verification to guard against false breakthroughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Build capability through related problem work rather than obsessing over famous unsolved problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on broadening skills by solving adjacent or smaller problems that develop techniques and intuition. This steady skill accumulation is more productive than fixating on a single famous problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical progress rewards sustained concentration over time, not innate talent or miraculous insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a long-horizon view of your career and research projects; prioritize sustained effort and incremental improvement over attempting to demonstrate instant brilliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth as a criterion for 'good' mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: A "good" piece of mathematics typically reflects months or years of patient elimination, not a single insight; readers should be able to feel that depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing research, aim for work that shows the elimination of false starts, development of tools, and accumulated refinement; such depth is what convinces readers of the result's value.
